title: Plainchant
hookLine: single-line melodies sung for centuries in monasteries: one voice, no harmony, no beat

cards: It's dark outside, well before dawn. In a stone chapel, men in black robes stand in two rows facing each other. Nobody plays an instrument.
Nobody keeps a beat. One voice lifts a short phrase, and the whole row answers on the same notes, in unison, like one long breath shared by everybody. The other row answers back.
The melody climbs a little, rests, falls. No chorus, no harmony underneath. Just one line of sound moving through the room, with the words of a psalm riding on it.

teach.h: ONE LINE, NO HARMONY, NO BEAT.
teach.b: Gregorian chant is the old sung prayer of the Latin church, also called plainchant, or plainsong. It's one melody line, sung by everyone together, with no harmony and no fixed rhythm.
The rhythm comes from the words: a long word gets room, a short one moves on. Why Gregory?

teach.h: TRADITION: A DOVE AT GREGORY'S EAR.
teach.b: Tradition links the chant to Pope Gregory the Great, and old paintings show a dove at his ear, as if the Holy Spirit were singing the melodies to him while he wrote them down.
Some historians think the chant grew slowly, from many singers in many places, and was gathered under his name later. Either way, the name stuck. The words are often the Psalms.
Monks sang them through the hours of the day, from before dawn to nightfall, and the Psalms describe that rhythm themselves.

teach.h: SEVEN TIMES A DAY, THE PSALMS.
teach.b: In the King James Bible, Psalm 119 says: "Seven times a day do I praise thee." And the letter to the Ephesians speaks of "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord."
Here's what chant asks of a singer. Nobody stands out. There's no solo star, no harmony part for the good singers.
Everyone sings the same note at the same moment, so the voices blur into one. The aim is that the prayer is heard, not the people singing it.
Some Catholic monasteries still sing it through the day, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran choirs.

how: In Catholic monasteries and some cathedrals, the Psalms and parts of the Mass are still sung in Gregorian chant through the day; some Anglican and Lutheran communities sing plainsong too.

games.q: you're a monk in the choir. you have the best voice in the chapel, and you know it. what does chant ask of you?
o: sing louder so the others can follow.
add a harmony line above the melody.
sing the same note as everyone, and blend.
games.why: chant is sung in unison: one line, everyone on the same note at the same moment, so the voices blur into one prayer.

practice: If you have a recording of plainchant nearby, play it quietly and let the line carry you; if not, breathe in, and on the out-breath hum one low, easy note for as long as the breath lasts.
Hum again, the same note or one step higher, with no tune and no performance, and let the note do the work. If you pray, let a short line from a psalm ride on the hum.

wordCard.voice: Gregorian chant. Plainsong: one melody line, sung together in unison, with the rhythm of the words, carrying the Psalms through the hours of the day.

orig.note: Latin: plain song, the old name for chant sung as a single unaccompanied line.

carryVoice: Your line: one line, sung. No one voice has to stand out. That was day eight hundred forty-eight.
